title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows an AI coding and agent tool being used as an operational component inside a ransomware campaign. The attackers ran Cursor Agent, which itself ran a Claude Sonnet model, to assist with hands-on exploitation of ESXi environments across multiple victim organizations. The AI tool was not compromised or tricked into doing something outside its design in a technical sense, it was simply adopted by malicious operators as a productivity aid for attack tasks, the same way a legitimate penetration tester might use it.

The failure mode here is misuse rather than a model malfunction. The system produced outputs, likely reconnaissance queries, code, or exploitation guidance, in response to prompts from people conducting unauthorized intrusions. No safety mechanism is reported to have detected or interrupted that use. Catching this would have required either behavioral controls within the agent platform that could distinguish malicious from legitimate use, or monitoring by the platform operator for patterns consistent with intrusion activity, neither of which is reported to have been in place.

What is not established is whether Cursor's operator had any technical or policy means to prevent this use, and the reporting reflects the findings of security researchers rather than any legal finding about the attackers or any confirmed attribution beyond the medium-confidence cluster assessment.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments and is using an AI tool called Cursor Agent to conduct hands-on attacks. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators deployed the Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet to assist with exploitation across ten target organizations. The ransomware encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Aurora also created a custom scanning tool to identify ESXi hosts and vCenter servers within victim networks.

In a separate operation, researchers identified a second Aurora cluster with medium confidence attribution, operating across eight victim organizations in Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This cluster used different attack methods including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The investigation revealed multiple command and control servers, proxy servers, and the Aurora leak site domain, providing security professionals with indicators to identify and defend against these attacks.
